title: Trump SoHo: Inflated Sales Numbers to Deceive Buyers, New York AG Settlement (2010)
description_short: Trump SoHo: Inflated Sales Numbers to Deceive Buyers, New York AG Settlement (2010)
description_medium: A June 2010 report on Trump SoHo identified a substantial discrepancy between marketing statements and documents filed with the New York attorney general. An affidavit described sixty-two units under contract in the condominium-hotel, far below earlier claims that more than half the inventory had sold.
description_long: A June 2010 report on Trump SoHo identified a gap between the condominium-hotel's marketing and sales figures filed with New York's attorney general. An affidavit described 62 units under contract, far below earlier claims that more than half the building had sold. Executives and brokers offered explanations involving different sales phases, while the reporting questioned how those explanations fit the project's offering plan. The gap mattered because sales claims could shape prospective buyers' impression of demand. The available 2010 account does not document a later buyer settlement or establish that the attorney general obtained a particular repayment. Sales representations, any later civil settlement and a legal finding of knowing deception are separate matters. The documented issue here is the discrepancy in reported sales and the unanswered questions about how the figures were presented. A fuller account of any later settlement requires a source for that proceeding and its date.
notes: The supplied Real Deal report documents a June 2010 discrepancy between Trump SoHo marketing and sales figures, but not the 2011 attorney-general settlement described in the synopsis. A settlement record and date are needed to complete the event titled around that settlement.

title: Hatch Act Violations — RNC at White House, Pompeo Speech from Jerusalem
description_short: Hatch Act Violations — RNC at White House, Pompeo Speech from Jerusalem
description_medium: The Office of Special Counsel’s 2021 report reviewed Hatch Act complaints about senior Trump administration officials’ political activity during the 2020 Republican National Convention and election. OSC found violations by 13 officials, including two connected to the convention, but said the president and vice president were exempt from the Act and White House grounds were not categorically off limits for political events.
description_long: The 2020 Republican National Convention included political activity by senior Trump administration officials, including events on White House grounds and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s partisan address from Jerusalem during an official trip. In November 2021, the Office of Special Counsel published findings from its Hatch Act Unit investigation of complaints about the convention and other campaign activity. OSC found that 13 senior officials had violated the law, including two violations tied to the convention. It also clarified that the Hatch Act did not categorically bar political events on certain White House grounds and that President Donald Trump and Vice President Mike Pence were exempt from its restrictions. The report said some officials had used their official authority or influence to affect the 2020 election, while describing limits on enforcement after officials left government. Those findings concern covered officials and do not establish that Trump personally violated the Hatch Act. The report documents specific ethics findings and legal limits rather than treating every political event at the White House as unlawful.
notes: The linked OSC report confirms findings against 13 senior officials, including two violations connected with the convention, while stating that the president and vice president were exempt and White House grounds were not categorically barred. The description does not attribute an individual violation to Pompeo without the report's specific finding.

title: Trump Announces 2024 Presidential Campaign—First Candidate with 91 Criminal Charges
description_short: Trump Announces 2024 Presidential Campaign—First Candidate with 91 Criminal Charges
description_medium: On November 15, 2022, Donald Trump announced from Mar-a-Lago that he would run for president again in 2024. The launch came a week after the midterm elections, in which several candidates he endorsed lost key races. Family members and political allies attended; the campaign announcement began a new bid but did not establish the legal or political theories later associated with his candidacy.
description_long: Donald Trump announced his 2024 presidential campaign on November 15, 2022, in a speech at his Mar-a-Lago resort. It was his first campaign announcement after losing the 2020 election and followed midterms in which several candidates he endorsed had lost pivotal races. NBC News reported that family members and prominent supporters, including Roger Stone, Mike Lindell and former Representative Devin Nunes, attended. Trump framed the campaign as a “comeback,” criticized Joe Biden and repeated claims about corruption and election fraud. He also promised to reverse Biden-era policies on climate change and immigration. The announcement formally shifted Trump from speculation about another run to campaigning for the Republican nomination. Its timing prompted discussion among party leaders and donors, but the supplied article does not establish that the announcement was designed to affect any criminal investigation or that all later criminal charges existed at the time. The record documents the launch, speech and immediate political context without treating an asserted legal motive as fact.
notes: NBC News confirms the date, location, 2024 announcement, attendees and speech themes. The supplied material does not establish the campaign launch as a legal strategy or support the later 91-count framing at the time of announcement.

title: Trump Pressures Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Arizona Officials to Overturn Results
description_short: Trump Pressures Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Arizona Officials to Overturn Results
description_medium: After the 2020 election, Trump and allies pressured officials in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Arizona to reject, delay, or reverse certified results. The supplied account describes the effort as a campaign directed at elected officials in swing states. The linked Politico report documents the pressure tactics and the dispute over certification.
description_long: After the 2020 election, Donald Trump and allies pressured officials in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Arizona to reject, delay, or reverse certified results. The pressure formed part of a wider effort to challenge the outcome after votes had been counted. In Michigan, Republican state legislators faced demands connected to the certification process; similar efforts targeted officials in other closely contested states. The entry concerns attempts to influence public officials and the administration of an election, not a lawful recount that independently establishes fraud. The effort targeted state officials responsible for election administration, although their responses varied. The episode is important because certification is a central safeguard in the transfer of power, and attempts to overturn certified results can weaken confidence in elections even when they do not succeed.
